summary.text: A 50-year-old woman presented in February 2020 with a two-year history of intermittent painful swelling, facial asymmetry, cervical fistulation and bony enlargement of the left mandibular body, and reported paresthesia of the left inferior alveolar nerve. Repeated oral antibiotic therapy gave only a brief ease of symptoms, and a decayed left mandibular second premolar was extracted alio loco.

A CT scan in March 2020 showed diffuse enlargement of the left mandibular body over 9 cm with a maximal width of 2.1 cm and bone marrow attenuation. The leukocyte count was normal at 8.74/nL and C-reactive protein slightly increased at 8.0 mg/L. The left mandibular molars were removed for advanced periodontitis, and a trepan bur biopsy showed chronic inflammation with bone marrow fibrosis and excess bone formation.

After the results were discussed with her, a subtotal left hemimandibulectomy sparing the uninvolved condyle was performed in June 2020 with reconstruction by a CADCAM planned free vascularized fibula graft from the right side. Resection histology showed reactive new subperiostal bone formation compatible with osteomyelitis with proliferative periostitis. The course was uneventful and she was discharged 10 days after surgery; occlusion was perfect and maximum mouth opening was 3.5 cm.

Six months after surgery she returned with massive swelling of the reconstructed left mandible without a fistula. Imaging showed new appositional bone around the fibula transplant, a widely ossified graft with moth damage like lesions and left mandibular inflammatory activation on SPECT; leukocytes were 12.5 cells/nL and C-reactive protein 19.5 mg/L. Core biopsy histology revealed recurrence of the known chronic osteomyelitis, culture and PCR found no bacteria, and recurrent osteomyelitis with proliferative periostitis was diagnosed.

A single shot of ibandronate 6 mg was given as an off-label trial. Three months afterwards she no longer complained of discomfort. Pain and swelling markedly declined, no signs of inflammation were detected and leukocyte and CRP levels were normalized. Cone beam tomography, dated 6 months after ibandronate in the figure caption, showed fewer moth damage like lesions and stable periostal new bone formation.

In the further course she showed no signs of inflammation. After another 3 months the osteosynthesis material was partially removed and dental implants were inserted; biopsies of the fibular bone and periostal apposition showed vital bone with slight periostal fibrosis. Nine months after ibandronate she had no pain, swelling or other discomfort, and prosthetic rehabilitation was initialized.
